questions.source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Why can proximity to markets affect agricultural activity?
options: Products may need to reach processors, distributors or consumers.
Markets control the climate and soil type.
All agricultural products must be used where they are produced.
Farms can operate only inside large cities.
questions.correctFeedback: Access to markets matters because products must move to the next users in the supply chain.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about where products may need to travel after production.
questions.source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: What does it mean to describe Australian agriculture as diverse?
options: It includes different agricultural activities that contribute different products.
It produces only one type of raw material.
Every region carries out exactly the same activities.
It is limited to livestock production.
questions.correctFeedback: Diversity refers to the range of activities and products within agriculture.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory links agricultural diversity to several different activity areas and products.
questions.source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Why does agriculture have both economic and social value?
options: It supplies communities, supports livelihoods and links regional production to wider markets.
It removes the need for transport and processing.
It guarantees that every region produces the same goods.
It matters only when products are exported.
questions.correctFeedback: These contributions show how agriculture supports both economic activity and communities.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory explains that agriculture matters for communities, livelihoods and market connections, not only trade.
questions.source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

sections.title: The four dimensions of food security

authoringProvenance.method: Signed-in ChatGPT in the in-app browser; one named theory section at a time

questions.question: Which statement best describes food security?
options: Food is produced in large quantities, even if people cannot obtain it.
People have reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
Every household grows all of its own food.
Food is available for a short period during the year.
questions.correctFeedback: Food security requires reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Food security includes access, quality, sufficiency and reliability, not production alone.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: What does the availability dimension of food security examine?
options: Whether people understand food labels
Whether sufficient food of suitable quality is present
Whether every person eats the same diet
Whether food remains affordable for one household
questions.correctFeedback: Availability concerns whether sufficient food of suitable quality is present.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on whether food is present through production, stored supplies and supply systems.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: Which group is identified as contributing to food availability?
options: Production, stored supplies and wider supply systems
Diet, exercise and personal preferences
Income, advertising and packaging
Sanitation, health and cooking skills
questions.correctFeedback: The theory identifies production, stored supplies and supply systems as sources of availability.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Return to the sentence explaining how food may be made available.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: What does the access dimension mainly concern?
options: Whether food can be stored for several years
Whether people have the physical and economic resources to obtain suitable food
Whether enough food is produced nationally
Whether all food has the same nutritional value
questions.correctFeedback: Access concerns the physical and economic resources needed to obtain food.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Access is about people's ability to obtain available food.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: Why can food be available while some households still experience food insecurity?
options: Available food is always unsuitable for people.
Households may lack the physical or economic resources needed to obtain it.
Food availability prevents supply networks from operating.
Food security applies only to countries, not households.
questions.correctFeedback: Availability does not guarantee that every household has access to the food.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory separates the presence of food from people's ability to obtain it.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: What does utilisation examine?
options: How exports are ranked between countries
How food, diet, clean water, sanitation and health affect nutritional needs
How quickly food is transported to shops
How much land is used for production
questions.correctFeedback: Utilisation considers whether food and surrounding conditions allow nutritional needs to be met.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on the conditions that affect whether the body can gain nutritional value from food.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: Which situation best shows a problem with utilisation?
options: Food is present, but conditions prevent people from gaining its full nutritional value.
Food is stored before being transported.
People have enough resources to obtain suitable food.
Production and supply continue reliably over time.
questions.correctFeedback: Utilisation can be limited even when food is available and accessible.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the situation where food is present but nutritional needs may still not be met.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: What does stability mean in food security?
options: Only food production remains unchanged.
The other dimensions continue over time without a high risk of interruption or loss.
People obtain food once, regardless of what happens later.
All food is stored in one location.
questions.correctFeedback: Stability means availability, access and utilisation continue over time.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Stability is about the continuation of the other dimensions, not a single event.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: Why might a food supply be accessible but not stable?
options: It is available only through production.
People can obtain it now, but access may not continue over time.
It contains safe and nutritious food.
It is supported by clean water and sanitation.
questions.correctFeedback: Short-term access does not guarantee that access will continue.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Compare conditions that exist briefly with conditions that can be maintained.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: Why must all four dimensions be considered together?
options: Each dimension describes a separate type of farming.
Strong performance in one dimension does not guarantee food security.
Availability automatically creates access, utilisation and stability.
Stability replaces the need for the other three dimensions.
questions.correctFeedback: Food security can fail when even one connected dimension is weak.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The final paragraph explains why no single dimension is enough by itself.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

questions.question: Which group contains only threats to food systems identified in the theory?
options: Drought, soil degradation, supply-chain disruption and pest outbreaks
Packaging design, advertising, cooking styles and tourism
School timetables, housing design, sport and entertainment
Road colour, shop layout, clothing and furniture
questions.correctFeedback: These are all identified pressures that can affect food systems.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph for the authorised list of food-system threats.

questions.question: How can drought and water scarcity affect agricultural production?
options: They can reduce the water available to crops and livestock.
They always improve soil condition.
They prevent all pest and disease outbreaks.
They guarantee stable transport routes.
questions.correctFeedback: Drought and water scarcity can limit the water available for crops and livestock.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on the direct effect of reduced water availability.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: How can extreme weather affect a food system?
options: It can disrupt production and transport connections.
It affects only the appearance of food packaging.
It always increases soil quality.
It removes the need for planning.
questions.correctFeedback: Extreme weather can interrupt both production and the movement of food.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory links extreme weather with two major parts of the food system.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Why can supply-chain disruption cause problems even when food has already been produced?
options: It can affect the movement, availability and prices of food.
It changes all food into raw materials.
It prevents soil from supporting crops.
It automatically causes a disease outbreak.
questions.correctFeedback: Produced food still needs to move through supply pathways to reach markets and consumers.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about what happens after production when transport or distribution is interrupted.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: What is a possible long-term effect of soil degradation?
options: The soil may become less able to support future production.
Transport routes become more reliable.
Water availability always increases.
Pest risks disappear completely.
questions.correctFeedback: Soil degradation can reduce the soil's productive capacity over time.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on the relationship between soil condition and future production.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: What is the main purpose of biosecurity in a food system?
options: To reduce risks from harmful pests and diseases
To increase dependence on one supply route
To replace all soil conservation
To prevent every type of extreme weather
questions.correctFeedback: Biosecurity helps reduce risks from pests and diseases that may cause harm.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Biosecurity is connected specifically to biological threats.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Which statement best describes resilience?
options: Avoiding all change in a food system
Preparing for disruption, adapting, and continuing or recovering essential functions
Using one response for every possible threat
Producing food without transport or supply pathways
questions.correctFeedback: Resilience involves preparation, adaptation, continuation and recovery.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Resilience does not mean removing all change or using one fixed response.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Why can diverse production and supply pathways improve resilience?
options: They can reduce dependence on one source, route or method.
They guarantee that no disruption will occur.
They remove the need for monitoring and planning.
They make every threat affect the system in the same way.
questions.correctFeedback: Diversity can reduce reliance on a single part of the system.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory says diversity reduces dependence but does not remove every risk.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Which response is most closely matched to pest and disease risks?
options: Biosecurity
Soil conservation
Changing transport prices
Reducing all supply pathways
questions.correctFeedback: Biosecurity is designed to reduce risks from pests and diseases.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Match the biological threat with the response described in the theory.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: Why is no single resilience response enough for every food-system threat?
options: Different threats affect systems in different ways and responses may involve trade-offs.
Every threat has exactly the same cause.
Resilience applies only to water scarcity.
Planning removes the need for other responses.
questions.correctFeedback: Responses must match different threats, and each approach has limits and possible trade-offs.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The final paragraph explains why several connected approaches are needed.
questions.source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

questions.question: How does a cattle breed differ from a Bos grouping?
options: A breed is more specific than a broad Bos grouping.
A breed describes only the climate where cattle live.
A breed is another name for any crossbred animal.
A breed is identified only by coat thickness.
questions.correctFeedback: Bos indicus and Bos taurus are broad groupings, while a breed is a more specific classification.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory distinguishes broad Bos groupings from the more specific classification of breed.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Which adaptation is commonly discussed in connection with Bos indicus cattle?
options: Tolerance of tropical heat
Guaranteed high meat quality
A calm temperament in every animal
High performance in every environment
questions.correctFeedback: Heat tolerance is an adaptive trait commonly associated with Bos indicus cattle.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory links Bos indicus cattle with tropical adaptation, but it does not guarantee quality, temperament or performance.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Which visible feature may be a clue in some Bos indicus cattle?
options: A shoulder hump
A guaranteed thick winter coat
A breed name marked on the hide
Identical body shape in every animal
questions.correctFeedback: A shoulder hump can be a visible clue in some Bos indicus cattle.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory lists several possible visible clues, but it also explains that they vary among animals.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Why should a shoulder hump be treated as a clue rather than proof?
options: Not every animal shows every feature, and appearance alone cannot confirm classification.
Shoulder humps are found only in young cattle.
A photograph always changes an animal's body shape.
Visible features provide no useful information at all.
questions.correctFeedback: Visible features can assist observation, but variation means they cannot confirm breed or group by themselves.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory allows visible clues to be used carefully, while warning that they are not conclusive evidence.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Which statement about Bos taurus cattle is supported by the theory?
options: Bos taurus includes many breeds with temperate origins.
Every Bos taurus animal has a thick coat.
All Bos taurus cattle have the same body shape.
Bos taurus is the name of one specific breed.
questions.correctFeedback: Bos taurus is a broad grouping that includes many breeds with temperate origins.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory describes common patterns but stresses variation among breeds and individual cattle.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Why might a crossbred animal be difficult to classify from appearance?
options: It may show a mixture of visible features from different ancestry.
It will have no visible features at all.
Its breed records are always incorrect.
It must belong equally to every cattle breed.
questions.correctFeedback: Crossbred cattle may inherit mixed visible features, making appearance-based classification less reliable.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The difficulty comes from mixed inherited features, not from a complete absence of evidence.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: What can a photograph reliably support?
options: Careful observation of visible features
Proof of temperament
Proof of meat quality
Proof of production performance
questions.correctFeedback: A photograph can support observation, but it cannot prove temperament, meat quality or performance.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory clearly limits what can be concluded from a photograph.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Which evidence would strengthen a cattle classification?
options: Verified breed or pedigree records
One photograph taken from a distance
A guess based on ear size alone
An assumption based on the paddock location
questions.correctFeedback: Verified breed or pedigree records provide stronger evidence than appearance alone.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Reliable classification requires verified records and other relevant evidence, not a single visual clue or assumption.
questions.source: Drive lesson: Introduction to Beef Cattle and Breeds:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cBNBGd1jpLO6wOmw6-T0p7hsorXT8SyaGA9pbH2NWy8/edit; Meat & Livestock Australia: Seven tips for rebuilding a genetically superior herd: https://www.mla.com.au/news-and-events/industry-news/seven-tips-for-rebuilding-a-genetically-superior-herd/

questions.question: Which set of factors forms part of the whole production environment?
options: Climate, feed, water and parasite pressure
Coat colour, sale price, name and age
Breed label, photograph, fence type and paddock size
Temperament, meat quality, markings and horn shape
questions.correctFeedback: The theory identifies climate, feed, water and parasite pressure as important parts of the production environment.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Return to the final paragraph and locate the environmental factors listed there.

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to call one cattle group universally best?
options: Suitability depends on the environment, production purpose and available evidence.
Every cattle group has exactly the same adaptations.
Visible features prove that all cattle perform equally.
Production environments do not affect cattle suitability.
questions.correctFeedback: The most suitable cattle depend on the conditions, purpose and reliable evidence available.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The theory explains that adaptation is a match between the animal and the whole production environment.

questions.question: What is selective breeding?
options: Choosing parent animals using defined objectives so desired inherited traits are more likely in future generations
Choosing the largest animals without considering evidence
Changing an animal's environment to alter its inherited traits
Selecting cattle only by coat colour
questions.correctFeedback: Selective breeding uses planned parent selection to increase the likelihood of desired inherited traits in later generations.

The appearance of one selected animal only

All cattle perform identically when objectives are clear
Environmental conditions remove inherited variation

questions.question: Which is a useful criterion for comparing layer systems?
options: Movement and behaviour opportunities
Package advertising
Egg brand popularity
Farm logo design
questions.correctFeedback: Movement and behaviour opportunities are relevant to system comparison.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Choose a feature connected with housing, management or welfare evidence.

questions.question: Which broad feature is associated with barn systems?
options: Birds are housed indoors with shared floor space
Birds remain outdoors at all times
Birds are identified by egg colour
No monitoring is required
questions.correctFeedback: Barn systems generally house birds indoors with opportunities for movement within the building.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Review the broad descriptions of cage, barn and free-range systems.

questions.question: Which broad feature is associated with free-range systems?
options: Access to outdoor areas as well as shelter
No exposure to weather
No need for biosecurity
Guaranteed welfare outcomes
questions.correctFeedback: Free-range systems provide outdoor access along with shelter.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Outdoor access is a system feature, but it does not remove risks or guarantee outcomes.

questions.question: What is a possible trade-off of greater outdoor access?
options: More behaviour opportunities but greater weather or predator exposure
Less movement and no environmental exposure
Guaranteed disease prevention
No land management requirements
questions.correctFeedback: Outdoor access may increase behaviour opportunities while also creating exposure risks.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Review the trade-off paragraph and identify both a benefit and a limitation.

questions.question: What is a possible advantage of more enclosed housing?
options: Closer monitoring and environmental control
Guaranteed better welfare
No infrastructure costs
Complete removal of disease risk
questions.correctFeedback: Enclosed systems may support closer monitoring and environmental control.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Choose a realistic management advantage rather than a universal guarantee.

questions.question: Which is an animal-based welfare indicator?
options: Observed behaviour
Housing construction cost
Land area
Egg packaging
questions.correctFeedback: Behaviour provides direct evidence about how birds are responding.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Animal-based indicators focus on the birds themselves.

questions.question: Which is a resource or management indicator?
options: Access to feed and water
A claim that one system is best
Egg colour
Retail price
questions.correctFeedback: Access to feed and water is a resource indicator used in welfare assessment.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Choose evidence about what is provided or how the system is managed.

questions.question: Why does a system label not prove welfare?
options: Welfare requires evidence from multiple indicators
Every system produces identical outcomes
Labels include complete health records
One housing feature explains all animal responses
questions.correctFeedback: Welfare outcomes require combined animal-based and management evidence.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining why one resource or label is insufficient.

questions.question: What makes a conclusion about layer systems defensible?
options: Using common criteria, evidence, trade-offs and uncertainty
Claiming one system is always best
Using only one photograph
Ignoring management differences
questions.correctFeedback: A defensible conclusion uses consistent evidence and avoids universal rankings.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph describing the features of an evidence-based conclusion.
